I gathered point transect data on different songbird species in different=
=20

My main aim is to compare relative densities per species in these=20
fragments. I=92m not interested in comparing densities between species, o=
nly=20
within species between fragments. Therefore, I analyse my data separately=
=20
per species. However, I still have some basic questions and doubts and I=20=

hope you can help me with answering them.

First, I analysed densities by pooling all data per species (over years=20=

and seasons), stratifying per forest fragment (detection function=20
estimated per stratum, (1)). The histograms for some fragments revealed=20=

that another bin grouping and truncation distance would give a better fit=
.=20
Therefore, I decided to do the analyses also seperately per fragment (and=
,=20
of course, per species), making an individual decision for truncation and=
=20
grouping for each fragment and selecting the best model for each bird=20
species per fragment. I did this to test if the model, used for pooled=20=

data in the stratified analysis (see (1)), was robust. Densities estimate=

with pooled data (detection function per stratum) were very similar to th=
e=20
densities estimated when separate analyses per species/fragment were run,=
=20
except for those fragments where sample size was low (< 50 observations).=
=20
My feeling is that it is then more logic to keep to the pooled data=20
stratified per fragment. Is this correct? Or should I choose 1 model,=20
based on the smallest summed AIC=92s (sum of AIC values of all fragments =
for=20

If I want to compare the densities for one species between fragments per=20=

sample size per species per year is not large enough. I could stratify pe=
r=20

,=20
but this would mean I wouldn=92t get standard errors for the fragment =96=
=20

plot.

 plot-

messages.subject: complex data selection filter-programmation error?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm having a problem when using complex selection criteria in the data=20=

selection filter. I want to estimate the detection function by pooling=20=

over similar species as descriped in the help-function under 'Situations=20=

where post-stratification is useful'. I intered follwing information in=20=

the data selection filter (distance 5 beta version):

Observation layer - Species=3D'BA' or 'TA' (BA and TA being species)

The analysis is run with the observations of the species that is first=20=

defined in the filter (here: BA; if I put it in the order 'TA' or 'BA',=20=

then only TA is considered for analysis). If I type in Species=3D'BA'=20
and 'TA', distance takes all observations of all species in the dataset,=20=

incl. thiose not mentioned in the selection filter.

Please allow me to add another question, concerning the use of=20
stratification:
If number of observation per stratum are less than 50, is it then allowed=
=20
(and does it make sense) to do a stratified analysis with detection=20
function estimated per stratum if the AIC value is lower than in a=20
stratified analysis with global detection function? MCDS with stratum as=20=

covariate generally gives poor results (higher AIC values), probably=20
because the key function selected for is the uniform key, so I needed to=20=

choose the 2nd best model function (based on AIC) to run an MCDS. The onl=
y=20
other option would thus be to use a stratified analysis with global=20
detection function.

Thanks a lot for your help!

Val=E9rie

messages.subject: Re: complex data selection filter-programmation error?
messages.body_plain:
Valerie (and list):

The syntax for complex data filtering is very specific; and as you have s=
een, it
is possible to create a subset of your data that is not what you expect.

Please consult the Appendix of the Users Guide, where there are several p=
ages on
"Data Filter Properties Dialog," where there are several examples of comp=
lex
selection criteria (paginated at p.215 in manual released under D5.0 Rele=
ase
2).  The simple solution to the problem you provided is to specify the fi=
eld
name in *each* of your criteria; e.g.,

Species =3D 'BA' OR Species =3D 'TA'

(note I've also capitalized the logical operator "OR")  That should filte=
r your
data in the manner you expect.

Regarding your second question, yes it does make sense to use stratum-spe=
cific
detection functions if guided by a model selection criterion, even should=
 there
be low numbers of detections in some strata.  You will have a more
parameter-rich model, but perhaps that additional structure is necessary
because of differences in detectability among strata.  Note, for the data=
 poor
strata, you are likely to have greater uncertainty in your estimates of f=
(0)
(or h(0)) (because of few data to precisely estimate the detection functi=
on)
that will have a ripple effect upon your estimate of density (abundance) =
in
those strata.  You should also make some assessment of absolute fit by
consulting the goodness-of-fit statistics as well as the relative measure=
s of
AIC.

messages.subject: Re: Seabirds
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jorge, List,

When dealing with clustered populations, and treating clusters as the =
analysis units, the distance we need for analysis is the distance to the =
geometric center of the group (see IDS book, page 13). If you use the =
distance to the closest animal, you will tend to underestimate distances =
to the cluster, and likely to overestimate abundance.

Regarding your first question, which is likely mostly related to flying =
birds, take a look at pages 198-203 of IDS book. You might want to treat =
birds flying separately. Sometimes, though because of the fast movement =
they seem a considerable proportion of the population, the truth is that =
only a small fraction of the population is in flight at any one moment. =
An approach might be to separately estimate birds on the surface and =
birds flying, and then combining the two estimates. Other approaches are =
suggested in the above pages of IDS.

Also, be careful not to record as distance =3D 0 all birds flying if =
they, at some point, crossed the transect line, because you will tend to =
have too many 0 measurements and the modelling of the detection function =
might become impossible. If the animals cross the line well beyond the =
vessel it might be best to ignore them. This might be hard to do in =
practice, and some arbitrary distance rule needs to be set up; what you =
want is a rule that avoids a spike in the data that is not a reflection =
of the true detection function, but a consequence of the undetected =
movement due to the flying.

Hope it helps,

Tiago

messages.subject: Re: flying birds RE: [DIST-SAMP] Seabirds
messages.body_plain:
Mark Tasker's snapshot method is fine provided the observers can=20
estimate reliably where the boundaries of the counting box are, and=20
quickly count all the birds within it (so there isn't time for many=20
birds to fly in and out).  As Tiago noted, there is a discussion of=20
these issues on pp198-203 of the Introduction to Distance Sampling=20
book.  Where densities are too great to allow distance sampling, then=20
counts within a narrow strip together with strip-count estimation=20
methods is probably the sensible option for birds on the sea.  For=20
flying birds, options are (1) Tasker's snapshot counts;  (2) record=20
flying birds as within the strip for a strip count when they pass abeam=20
of the boat, provided they are still in the strip at that time (if they=20
have flown beyond the strip by then, they're not counted);  (3) estimate=20
separately the proportion of time birds spend on the sea, then divide=20
the estimated number of birds on the sea by this proportion.

Steve Buckland
